learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how and why countries exchange goods and services, and understand the massive networks that keep global markets connected!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Countries trade because resources are unevenly distributed. Differences in climate, geology, mineral resources, and economic development make trade mutually beneficial.
The difference between a country's exports and imports. If exports > imports, it's a Favorable (Positive) Balance. If imports > exports, it's an Unfavorable (Negative) Balance.
An international organization set up in 1995 to regulate and facilitate global trade, remove tariffs, and settle trade disputes between member nations.

Ports handle the bulk of international cargo. They provide docking, loading, unloading, and storage facilities. They are classified by cargo type (industrial, commercial, comprehensive) and location (inland, outports).
While trade boosts economies, it can also lead to exploitation of developing countries, environmental degradation (pollution, resource depletion), and the spread of diseases.

fun_activity.title: 🔄 The Barter Game
fun_activity.instructions: Imagine money doesn't exist. You have 5 extra notebooks and you want a pizza. How many trades with your friends would it take to get from notebooks to a pizza? This is why currency was invented to replace the barter system!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly define 'Balance of Trade' and distinguish between favorable and unfavorable balances.
📌 Be ready to classify ports (e.g., Entrepot ports, Naval ports, Oil ports) with real-world examples.
📌 Understand the role of the WTO and the criticisms against it (e.g., favoring developed nations).
quick_recap: ⭐ The ancient Silk Route was an early example of long-distance international trade.
⭐ Bilateral trade is between two countries; Multilateral trade involves many trading partners.
⭐ Ports are called the 'gateways' of international trade because almost all heavy cargo passes through them.
